title: Incorruptibles, honestly
hookLine: some saints' bodies decay less than expected; the Church does not treat this as proof

lines: A NUN IN A GLASS CASE.
cards: A glass case in a side chapel. Inside, a nun lies as if asleep, hands folded, face calm. A sign says she died long ago.
Tourists lean in close. One whispers that it's a miracle. Another whispers that it must be wax.
A child asks, loudly, whether she's real. Nobody quite knows what to say. Here's what neither whisperer may expect: the Catholic Church doesn't count this as proof of anything.
Not of holiness, not of a miracle, not of the faith.

teach.b: Incorruptibles is the name people give to saints whose bodies, when their tombs were opened, had decayed less than expected. The word sounds like a perfect body; the honest picture is often different.
Some are dried, darkened or partly preserved, and some on display have faces and hands covered with wax or a mask, which some shrines say openly when asked. Next, what the Church does with it.
Investigating a candidate for sainthood, it looks at a life of heroic virtue and at miracles attributed to the person's prayers after death, such as healings doctors cannot explain.
A preserved body isn't on that list. Saints' remains have also decayed in the ordinary way, and that counts against no one. So the Church's posture is careful: interesting, worth studying, not proof.
Then, why honor the remains at all. The body matters in Catholic belief.
Paul writes of the resurrection of the dead, in the Douay-Rheims: "It is sown in corruption, it shall rise in incorruption." The hope isn't a body that stays fresh in a glass case.
It's that God raises the dead, whatever state the tomb is in. A decayed saint and a preserved saint share the same promise. Last, honesty itself.
Some cases have natural explanations: dry air, the burial place, embalming. Some are still debated.
A Catholic is free to say, calmly, we don't know.
Faith that needed a perfect corpse to stand up would be fragile, and the Church doesn't ask anyone to lean on it.

how: Catholics venerate the relics of saints, including some whose bodies are displayed in churches; the Church does not treat a body's preservation as a miracle or as evidence in canonization, which looks at heroic virtue and miracles attributed to the saint's intercession.

o: relics sealed in wax so they never decay
saints whose bodies decayed less than expected
saints whose bodies are proof of their holiness

p: heroic virtue and miracles after death

s: the Church counts an incorrupt body as a miracle for canonization
canonization looks at heroic virtue and miracles attributed to a saint's prayers. a preserved body isn't on the list.
some displayed saints have wax or a mask over the face
some shrines say so openly when asked.
a saint whose body decayed is less holy
saints' remains have also decayed in the ordinary way. it counts against no one.

games.q: a saint's tomb is opened and the body is found remarkably preserved. people start calling it proof. what does the Church do?
o: declare it a miracle at once.
study it with interest, and decline to call it proof.
close the tomb and forbid any talk of it.
games.why: the Church treats it as interesting and worth study, and does not count it as proof of holiness or of the faith.

practice: Bring to mind one real open question, about faith or the world, that you can't answer; not a debate you want to win.

Notice any pull to settle it fast, obviously yes or obviously no, let the pull pass, and say quietly, I don't know yet. If you pray, offer the question to God as it is, unfinished; if you don't, just let it stay open.

wordCard.voice: Incorruptibles. Saints whose bodies decayed less than expected. Honored, studied, and never treated by the Church as proof. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek of 1 Corinthians 15:42: incorruption, what Paul says the dead are raised in.

carryVoice: Your line: not proof. Honored, studied, and held calmly, with nothing leaning on it. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: It is sown in corruption, it shall rise in incorruption.
